title: Google brings Gemini computer use to Mac in a background window
subtitle: A Mac-only beta lets Gemini drive desktop apps in an isolated window for paid Google AI subscribers on Apple Silicon, with prompt-injection warnings in the docs.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google rolled out computer use in the Gemini Mac app this week, available in English in the U.S. to adult users on Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra personal plans. The feature requires an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later. Users open the Mac app, enter Task mode and prompt with @Computer use. The agent runs in an isolated background window so the main cursor and display stay free; users can watch a live preview in the chat and interrupt. Work and school accounts are excluded at launch, and Google has not announced Windows or Chromebook support.

Sensitive actions require confirmation, and apps the user marks 'always allow' skip the per-app prompt. Google's documentation carries a prompt-injection warning — text on a page or in an email the agent reads can try to override the user's instructions, and Google tells users to assume that risk when they grant access. That warning is doing more work than it looks like. Any computer-use agent inherits the full attack surface of the apps it drives, which means the operating system's permission model is now part of the model's prompt.

The release landed the same week Anthropic moved Claude's computer use out of research preview and into a Team and Enterprise beta. Two things are happening at once: the major labs are converging on the same product category — an agent that sees the screen and operates desktop apps — and they are converging on the same mitigations: isolated windows, admin allow lists, per-action confirmations. That convergence suggests the hard problems are now security and UX, not capability.

A note for learners: the promise of 'computer use' is that you stop writing scripts for repetitive work and just describe the outcome. The failure mode is that a hostile page gets the agent to do something you did not describe. If you try it, start with a sandboxed account, turn off always-allow, and treat the first week as a security exercise: what does the agent do when you paste in something from an untrusted source? That answer is more important than any demo.
